title: AT&T Mobility LLC v. Concepcion (2011)
summary: The Court held that the FAA preempted the California rule used to require class procedures contrary to the arbitration agreement.
notes:
The assigned chapter discusses continuing questions about generally applicable defenses and class waivers.

The Concepcions were charged $30.22 in sales tax on phones advertised as free; the district court denied AT&T's motion to compel arbitration under California's Discover Bank rule and the Ninth Circuit affirmed; the Supreme Court (Scalia, J., 5-4) reversed and remanded, with Justice Thomas concurring and Justice Breyer's dissent joined by Justices Ginsburg, Sotomayor and Kagan.

sections.Parties: Customers sued AT&T over a charge associated with a promotion described as providing a free phone.
sections.Material Facts: The individual charge was small. The agreement required arbitration and individual rather than class proceedings. California’s rule would treat the class waiver as unconscionable in the circumstances. The company invoked the Federal Arbitration Act to enforce the agreed procedure.
sections.Procedural History: The dispute over compelling arbitration reached the Supreme Court, which rejected application of the state rule by a five-to-four vote.
sections.Issue: Could the state unconscionability rule be applied to invalidate the class waiver in the arbitration agreement?
sections.Holding: No under the Court’s FAA preemption analysis.
sections.Reasoning: The majority regarded the move from bilateral to class arbitration as a fundamental procedural change involving absentees, additional formality, greater stakes, and limited judicial review. Requiring that change by state law conflicted with the federal arbitration framework as the Court understood it. The agreement’s role and the structure of arbitration were central, while the desirability of preserving small claims could not by itself override the federal statute.

learning.why: The Court held that the FAA preempted the California rule used to require class procedures contrary to the arbitration agreement.

topics.cp-class-waiver: The Federal Arbitration Act displaced the state rule used to invalidate the class-arbitration waiver.
topics.cp-federal-preemption: A state rule could conflict with the federal arbitration framework despite its consumer-protection purpose.
topics.cp-access: The separate opinions disagreed about small-value claims and the consequences of individualized arbitration.
topics.cp-class-actions: The decision governs whether class procedures can be required over an arbitration agreement, a threshold question for consumer class litigation.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Breyer’s dissent emphasized that low-value claims may never be pursued individually and defended the state’s assessment of unfair terms in that setting.

mnemonic.rationale: A free phone with sales tax
